title: Agrestes Lycii
titleEn: Latona and the Lycian Peasants — Metamorphoses VI.313–381
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Shaken by the anger the goddess has just shown, the crowd falls to retelling older stories about her, and one bystander offers this one. Driven from her childbed and parched with thirst in Lycia, Latona knelt at a small pool to drink and was refused by the peasants gathering reeds there, who churned the water to mud rather than let her take any. The tale reaches us at two removes — a traveller reporting what a local host told him at an altar standing in the middle of a lake — and it ends with the peasants still quarrelling, under water.

sentences.t:
Tum vero cuncti manifestam numinis iram
femina virque timent cultuque impensius omnes
magna gemelliparae venerantur numina divae,
utque fit, a facto propiore priora renarrant.
sentences.l: Then indeed all, woman and man, fear the manifest anger of the divine power, and all with more lavish worship venerate the great godhead of the twin-bearing goddess, and, as happens, from the nearer deed they retell earlier ones.
sentences.i: Then every one of them, woman and man alike, fears the goddess's anger now plainly shown, and all worship the great power of the twin-bearing goddess with more devotion than before; and, as people do, the latest event starts them retelling older ones.
sentences.n: The close of one story and the door into the next. 'numinis iram' is the goddess's anger, called 'manifest' because it has just been seen. 'gemelliparae' — 'twin-bearing' — is a coined compound of the kind Ovid enjoys, and it names her by the one fact about her that matters here. The last line states the poem's own method out loud: a recent event reminds the crowd of older ones, and an inset tale begins.

sentences.t:
E quibus unus ait: “Lyciae quoque fertilis agris
non impune deam veteres sprevere coloni.
sentences.l: One out of them says: 'In the fields of fertile Lycia too the farmers of old scorned the goddess, not unpunished.
sentences.i: One of them says: 'In the fields of fertile Lycia too the farmers of long ago scorned the goddess — and did not get away with it.
sentences.n: 'E quibus unus' hands the narration to an anonymous bystander; everything from here to the end of the part is his voice, with a second speaker nested inside it. 'sprevere' = 'spreverunt': the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for -erunt, which you will meet on nearly every page. 'non impune' is litotes, understatement by negation — 'not unpunished' means they paid dearly.

sentences.t:
Res obscura quidem est ignobilitate virorum,
mira tamen.
sentences.l: The affair is obscure indeed, from the lowness of the men, but marvellous all the same.
sentences.i: It is an obscure story, admittedly — the men in it were nobodies — but a marvellous one.
sentences.n: 'ignobilitate' is an ablative of cause: the story is little known because of the low birth of the men in it. 'quidem … tamen' is the standard concessive pair, 'granted X, but Y'. The speaker is apologising for his material before he begins, which is itself a storyteller's move.

sentences.t:
Vidi praesens stagnumque locumque
prodigio notum.
sentences.l: I saw, being present myself, both the pool and the place known for the marvel.
sentences.i: I was there and saw it myself — the pool, and the spot famous for the wonder.
sentences.n: 'praesens' is an adjective agreeing with the subject where English wants an adverb or a clause: 'I, on the spot, saw'. Latin very often puts as an adjective what English puts elsewhere. 'prodigio' is another ablative of cause. The claim of eyewitness is what licenses the whole inset story.

sentences.t:
Nam me iam grandior aevo
impatiensque viae genitor deducere lectos
iusserat inde boves gentisque illius eunti
ipse ducem dederat.
sentences.l: For my father, by now rather advanced in years and unequal to the road, had ordered me to bring away picked cattle from there, and had himself given me, as I went, a guide of that people.
sentences.i: My father, by then well on in years and not up to the journey, had sent me to fetch choice cattle from there, and gave me a man of that country as a guide for the trip.
sentences.n: 'grandior aevo' is a comparative with an ablative of respect — 'greater as to age', i.e. getting old. 'impatiens viae' is literally 'not enduring of the road'. 'eunti' is a present participle in the dative, standing alone for an unexpressed 'mihi' — the person 'dederat' gives the guide to: 'to me as I went'. The same 'me' cannot serve both verbs, since 'iusserat' needs it accusative; Latin lets the participle carry the second case by itself. Latin packs into one word what English needs a clause for, and it will do this constantly.

sentences.t:
Cum quo dum pascua lustro,
ecce lacu medio sacrorum nigra favilla
ara vetus stabat tremulis circumdata cannis.
sentences.l: While I range over the pastures with him — look — in the middle of a lake an old altar was standing, black with the ash of sacrifices, ringed about with trembling reeds.
sentences.i: While I was going the rounds of the pasture with him — and there it was: in the middle of a lake an old altar, black with sacrificial ash, ringed with quivering reeds.
sentences.n: 'Cum quo' opening the sentence is a connecting relative — it means 'and with him', not 'with whom'. Latin habitually starts a new sentence with a relative pronoun where English starts one with a pronoun (you have already met one in 'E quibus unus' above); you will see this constantly, and it is flagged again at 352. 'dum' with a present indicative ('lustro') is regular Latin for 'while' even inside past narrative, and English has to shift it to a past tense. 'ecce' is the storyteller's pointing finger. 'nigra favilla' is ablative of cause with 'nigra' agreeing with 'ara'; 'circumdata cannis' is a perfect passive participle with an ablative, 'surrounded by reeds'. The altar's ash proves the place is still in use.

sentences.t:
Restitit et pavido “faveas mihi” murmure dixit
dux meus; et simili “faveas” ego murmure dixi.
sentences.l: My guide stopped and in a frightened murmur said 'be gracious to me'; and in a like murmur I said 'be gracious'.
sentences.n: 'faveas' is an optative subjunctive — a prayer rather than a command: 'may you be favourable'. The repetition is the whole point of the couplet: the local man utters the formula, and the traveller, who has no idea whose altar this is, echoes it back without the 'mihi' — he has the words and not the prayer. Note how 'dux meus' is held back to the start of the next line, a favourite Ovidian delay.

sentences.t:
Naiadum Faunine foret tamen ara rogabam
indigenaeve dei, cum talia rettulit hospes:
sentences.l: Still I was asking whether the altar was of the Naiads or of Faunus or of a native god, when my host reported such things as these:
sentences.i: I was asking all the same whose altar it was — the Naiads', Faunus's, or some god of the place — when my host told me this:
sentences.n: An indirect question: 'foret' (an alternative form of 'esset') is subjunctive because it depends on 'rogabam'. The '-ne … -ve' pair sets out the alternatives, 'whether … or'. 'Naiadum', 'Fauni' and 'dei' are all possessive genitives — whose altar it is. 'hospes' is the guest-host word, covering either party in the relationship; here it is the local man.

sentences.t: “Non hac, o iuvenis, montanum numen in ara est:
sentences.l: 'It is not a mountain divinity, young man, that is on this altar:
sentences.n: The second level of speech opens. The bystander who began at 317 is telling what happened to him in Lycia, and here he quotes his host, so from this line to 381 we are inside a speech within a speech — and Latona's own words at 349 will make a third level inside that. The edition marks this only by opening a fresh quotation here and closing two at 381. 'hac … in ara' is split around the vocative — Ovid separates prepositions from their nouns freely. The correction matters: the traveller has been guessing at small local gods, and he is about to be told this belongs to an Olympian.

sentences.t:
illa suam vocat hanc, cui quondam regia coniunx
orbem interdixit, quam vix erratica Delos
orantem accepit, tum cum levis insula nabat.
sentences.l: she calls this one her own, she to whom the royal wife once forbade the world, whom wandering Delos scarcely received as she begged, at the time when the island floated light on the water.
sentences.i: she calls this altar her own — the goddess the royal wife once shut out of the whole world, whom drifting Delos barely took in when she pleaded, back when the island still floated free.
sentences.n: Two relative clauses and a participle in a row, all pointing at the same person, and none of them names her: 'cui', then 'quam', then 'orantem' agreeing with 'quam'. 'orbem interdixit' takes a dative of the person barred and an accusative of the thing barred — 'forbade the world to her'. 'regia coniunx', 'the royal wife', is Juno, named by title only. Delos was said to drift on the sea until it anchored itself to receive this birth.

sentences.t:
Illic incumbens cum Palladis arbore palmae
edidit invita geminos Latona noverca.
sentences.l: There, leaning on a palm along with the tree of Pallas, Latona brought forth twins, their stepmother unwilling.
sentences.i: There, propped against a palm and Pallas's olive, Latona gave birth to the twins, though their stepmother was against it.
sentences.n: 'invita … noverca' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X in such a state' phrase where English wants a whole clause: 'though their stepmother was against it'. Expect this construction everywhere. 'Palladis arbor' is the olive, named by its owning divinity rather than by its own name, which is standard poetic manner. 'noverca' is Juno, stepmother to the children because Jupiter is their father, and the word carries the full Roman stereotype of the hostile stepmother.

sentences.t:
Hinc quoque Iunonem fugisse puerpera fertur
inque suo portasse sinu, duo numina, natos.
sentences.l: From here too the new mother is said to have fled Juno and to have carried in her own bosom her sons, two divinities.
sentences.i: From there too, they say, the new mother fled from Juno, carrying her sons — two gods — at her breast.
sentences.n: 'fertur' with an infinitive is 'she is said to have…', the standard way of reporting legend without vouching for it. 'fugisse' and 'portasse' are perfect infinitives, the second a syncopated form of 'portavisse'. 'duo numina' stands in apposition to 'natos' — the infants are already gods. 'quoque' here is the adverb 'also'; watch out for the other 'quo-que', 'and with which', which looks identical on the page.

sentences.t:
Iamque Chimaeriferae, cum sol gravis ureret arva,
finibus in Lyciae longo dea fessa labore
sidereo siccata sitim conlegit ab aestu,
uberaque ebiberant avidi lactantia nati.
sentences.l: And now, in the territory of Chimaera-bearing Lycia, when the heavy sun was burning the fields, the goddess, wearied by long toil and dried by the starry heat, gathered thirst, and her greedy children had drunk dry her milk-giving breasts.
sentences.i: And now in the country of Lycia, home of the Chimaera, with the sun beating down on the fields, the goddess — worn out by the long journey and parched by the blaze of the sky — grew thirsty; and her hungry babies had drained her milky breasts.
sentences.n: 'sitim conlegit' — 'gathered thirst' — is an odd and physical idiom: the thirst accumulates in her rather than striking her. 'labor' here is toil and travel — the hardship of the flight from Juno with the twins, not childbirth: the birth was on Delos, several stages back. 'siccata' is a perfect passive participle agreeing with 'dea', 'dried out'. 'Chimaeriferae' is another coined compound, naming the region by the monster it produced. 'ureret' is imperfect subjunctive in a circumstantial 'cum' clause — the burning is the whole setting, not just the time. The pluperfect 'ebiberant' places the nursing before the thirst: it is her own milk that has emptied her.

sentences.t:
Forte lacum mediocris aquae prospexit in imis
vallibus; agrestes illic fruticosa legebant
vimina cum iuncis gratamque paludibus ulvam.
sentences.l: By chance she caught sight of a lake of middling water down in the low valleys; peasants there were gathering bushy osiers along with rushes and the sedge that is pleasing to marshes.
sentences.i: By chance she spotted a smallish pool of water low down in the valleys; countrymen were there gathering shoots of willow along with rushes and the sedge that thrives in marshland.
sentences.n: 'mediocris aquae' is a genitive of description — a lake 'of middling water', not much of a lake. 'gratam paludibus' is an adjective with a dative: the sedge likes the swamp, and one word does the botany. These are the 'agrestes' of the edition's heading for this part, and their work with reeds is exactly the work of people who live off standing water.

sentences.t:
Accessit positoque genu Titania terram
pressit, ut hauriret gelidos potura liquores.
sentences.l: The Titan's daughter drew near and, her knee set down, pressed the earth, so that she might draw up the chill waters, about to drink.
sentences.i: The Titaness came up and went down on one knee to the ground, meaning to reach for a drink of the cold water.
sentences.n: 'Titania' — 'daughter of a Titan' — names her by descent, from Coeus, who is named at last later on. 'posito genu' is another ablative absolute. 'potura' is a future active participle expressing intention, 'meaning to drink': Latin has a participle tense English simply lacks, and it usually has to become a clause or an infinitive.

sentences.t: Rustica turba vetat. Dea sic adfata vetantes:
sentences.l: The country crowd forbids it. Thus the goddess addressed those forbidding:
sentences.i: The country crowd says no. The goddess spoke to them as they blocked her:
sentences.n: Historic present ('vetat') standing beside a perfect ('adfata') — Ovid moves in and out of the present to quicken and slow a scene, and English renders both as past. 'vetantes' is a present participle used as a noun, 'the ones who are forbidding'. 'adfata' keeps this edition's 'adf-' spelling where later texts print 'aff-'.

sentences.t: “Quid prohibetis aquis? usus communis aquarum est.
sentences.l: 'Why do you keep me from the waters? The use of waters is common.
sentences.i: 'Why do you keep me from the water? Water is for everyone's use.
sentences.n: 'prohibetis aquis' uses an ablative of separation — 'you fence me off from the water' — with the person barred left understood. 'usus communis' is language out of Roman legal thinking about things nobody owns: running water is a thing held in common. She opens not with her divinity but with an argument, and she argues like a litigant.

sentences.t:
Nec solem proprium natura nec aera fecit
nec tenues undas: ad publica munera veni.
sentences.l: Nature made neither the sun a private thing, nor the air, nor the thin waters: I have come to public gifts.
sentences.i: Nature made no one the owner of the sun, or the air, or the clear water: what I have come to is public property.
sentences.n: 'proprium' is predicative and governs all three accusatives — nature made none of them anyone's own. 'aera' is a Greek accusative of 'aer'; Greek nouns keep Greek endings in Latin verse. 'munera' are 'gifts' in the sense of things granted to everyone, and 'publica' is the exact legal opposite of 'proprium'. 'tenues undas' is 'thin waters' in the physical sense — clear, unclouded — which is going to matter shortly.

sentences.t: Quae tamen ut detis, supplex peto.
sentences.l: Yet that you give these things, I ask as a suppliant.
sentences.i: All the same, I am asking you for them as a suppliant.
sentences.n: 'Quae' is a connecting relative opening the sentence — 'and these things' — not a question and not a real relative clause. It is one of the commonest joins in Latin, and English just uses a pronoun. 'ut detis' is a substantive clause after 'peto', 'I ask that you give'. Having just argued that she has a right to the water, she asks for it as a favour; the shift is deliberate.

sentences.t:
Non ego nostros
abluere hic artus lassataque membra parabam,
sed relevare sitim.
sentences.l: I was not preparing to wash my limbs here and my wearied members, but to relieve my thirst.
sentences.i: I was not getting ready to wash my body here, my tired limbs — only to ease my thirst.
sentences.n: 'nostros' is the plural for 'meos', common in verse and not really a royal plural. 'artus' and 'membra' are near-synonyms doubled for weight, which Latin verse does constantly where English would say it once. Both infinitives hang on 'parabam'. She is answering an objection nobody has made: she will not dirty their water.

sentences.t:
Caret os umore loquentis
et fauces arent, vixque est via vocis in illis.
sentences.l: The mouth of me speaking lacks moisture, and my throat is dry, and there is scarcely a way for my voice in them.
sentences.i: My mouth is dry even as I speak, my throat is parched, and my voice can hardly find a way through.
sentences.n: 'careo' takes an ablative of the thing lacked, 'umore'. 'loquentis' is a present participle in the genitive agreeing with an unexpressed 'mei' — 'of me as I speak'; Latin can drop the pronoun and let the participle carry it. 'illis' is plural because it picks up 'fauces', a noun Latin uses only in the plural where English has a single 'throat' — hence the literal's 'in them'. 'via vocis' is a physical image: the voice needs a passage, and the dry throat has closed it. The speech is describing its own difficulty as it is made.

sentences.t:
Haustus aquae mihi nectar erit, vitamque fatebor
accepisse simul: vitam dederitis in unda.
sentences.l: A draught of water will be nectar to me, and I shall confess that I have received life along with it: you will have given life in the water.
sentences.i: A drink of water will be nectar to me, and I will admit I have been given my life with it: in that water you will have given me life.
sentences.n: 'mihi' is a dative of reference, 'so far as I am concerned'. 'fatebor … accepisse' is indirect statement — accusative and infinitive after a verb of saying, with 'me' understood as its subject. 'dederitis' is future perfect: the gift will already be complete at the moment she drinks. Nectar is the drink of the gods, so the compliment is precise rather than merely warm: plain water will be to her what the divine drink is.

sentences.t:
Hi quoque vos moveant, qui nostro bracchia tendunt
parva sinu:”
sentences.l: Let these too move you, who stretch out their small arms from my bosom:'
sentences.i: Let these move you as well, holding out their little arms from my breast:'
sentences.n: 'moveant' is a jussive subjunctive, a third-person command — 'let them move you'. 'parva' is neuter plural and belongs to 'bracchia', not to 'sinu', which is masculine; Ovid throws it to the head of the next line, far from its noun, so that the small word lands alone. 'nostro … sinu' is an ablative of place from which. This is her last argument, and it is not an argument at all. Magnus closes her speech at the colon here, and the English closes it with her.

sentences.t: et casu tendebant bracchia nati.
sentences.l: and by chance the children were stretching out their arms.
sentences.n: 'casu' is an ablative of manner, 'as it happened'. One word deflates the whole appeal: the babies are not pleading, they are simply moving, and it is the mother who turns the movement into a plea. 'tendebant' is imperfect — the arms go out and stay out.

sentences.t: Quem non blanda deae potuissent verba movere?
sentences.l: Whom could the goddess's coaxing words not have moved?
sentences.n: A rhetorical question with its answer built in: nobody. 'potuissent' is a past potential subjunctive, 'could have'. This is the narrator stepping out of the story to comment, and its work is to set up the flat contradiction that opens the next sentence — 'these men, however'.

sentences.t:
Hi tamen orantem perstant prohibere minasque,
ni procul abscedat, conviciaque insuper addunt.
sentences.l: These men nevertheless persist in fending off the one praying, and add on top threats, if she does not withdraw far off, and abuse.
sentences.i: These men, though, go on blocking her as she pleads, and add threats on top of it — if she will not clear off — and insults.
sentences.n: 'orantem' is a participle standing as a noun, 'her as she begs'. 'perstant prohibere' takes a plain infinitive. 'ni procul abscedat' is the content of the threat, in the subjunctive because it is being reported as their words rather than stated as fact. 'convicia' is the strong word here — not disagreement but abuse — and it will come back much later as the frogs' permanent noise.

sentences.t:
Nec satis est, ipsos etiam pedibusque manuque
turbavere lacus imoque e gurgite mollem
huc illuc limum saltu movere maligno.
sentences.l: Nor is that enough: they even churned the waters themselves with feet and with hand, and from the deepest of the pool they moved the soft mud this way and that with a spiteful leap.
sentences.i: And that was not enough: they churned up the pool itself with their feet and their hands, and with spiteful leaping dragged the soft mud this way and that from the bottom.
sentences.n: 'turbavere' and 'movere' are both third-plural perfects in -ere (= 'turbaverunt', 'moverunt'); 'movere' is spelled exactly like the present infinitive 'to move' and is not it — only the sense of the sentence tells you. 'maligno' is the moral word: the leap is not play but ill-will. Note what they are destroying — the 'tenues undas', the clear water she named in her own argument.

sentences.t:
Distulit ira sitim: neque enim iam filia Coei
supplicat indignis nec dicere sustinet ultra
verba minora dea, tollensque ad sidera palmas
“aeternum stagno” dixit “vivatis in isto.”
sentences.l: Anger put off thirst: for the daughter of Coeus no longer entreats the unworthy, nor does she bring herself to speak further words lesser than a goddess, and raising her palms to the stars she said, 'may you live for ever in that pool of yours.'
sentences.i: Anger put her thirst aside: the daughter of Coeus no longer begs of men who do not deserve it, nor can she bring herself to say another word beneath a goddess; and lifting her hands to the stars she said, 'live for ever in that pool of yours.'
sentences.n: 'Distulit ira sitim' turns the whole story in three words. 'verba minora dea' has an ablative of comparison — words 'lesser than a goddess', beneath her rank. 'indignis' is a dative with 'supplicat', and it is her judgement of them rather than a neutral description. 'vivatis' is a jussive subjunctive doing duty as the curse itself, and 'isto' is the demonstrative of the second person — 'that pool of yours' — carrying the contempt that form can carry. The metamorphosis is spoken, not performed.

sentences.t:
Eveniunt optata deae: iuvat esse sub undis
et modo tota cava submergere membra palude,
sentences.l: The goddess's wishes come out true: it is a pleasure to be under the waves and now to sink all the limbs in the hollow marsh,
sentences.i: The goddess's wish comes true: they enjoy being under water — now sinking their whole bodies in the hollow marsh,
sentences.n: 'iuvat' is impersonal, 'it pleases', with the infinitives as its subject, so the new life is described without a grammatical subject at all — which is precisely the effect: the men have stopped being anybody in particular. 'optata' is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, 'the things wished'. The change itself is never announced; it is simply visible in what the creatures now do.

sentences.t:
nunc proferre caput, summo modo gurgite nare,
saepe super ripam stagni consistere, saepe
in gelidos resilire lacus.
sentences.l: now to put out the head, now to swim at the top of the pool, often to stand on the bank of the pond, often to leap back into the cold waters.
sentences.i: now poking their heads out, now swimming on the surface, often perching on the edge of the pool, often jumping back into the cold water.
sentences.n: Still more infinitives hanging on that one 'iuvat', strung along with 'modo … nunc … modo … saepe … saepe': the rhythm of the list is the restlessness of frogs. 'summo gurgite' is an ablative of place, 'at the top of the water'. 'resilire', 'leap back', is the word that makes them unmistakable several lines before the poem uses the noun.

sentences.t:
Sed nunc quoque turpes
litibus exercent linguas pulsoque pudore,
quamvis sint sub aqua, sub aqua maledicere temptant.
sentences.l: But even now they exercise their foul tongues in quarrels and, shame driven out, although they are under the water, under the water they try to speak evil.
sentences.i: But even now they keep their filthy tongues busy with quarrelling, and, all shame gone, though they are under water, under water they still try to curse.
sentences.n: 'pulso pudore' is an ablative absolute, 'with shame beaten out of them'. The repetition 'sub aqua, sub aqua' is both the joke and the point: the thing is impossible and they attempt it anyway. 'quamvis' takes the subjunctive, 'sint'. 'turpes' means base and ugly at the same time — a judgement on what the tongues say and, three lines from now, a description of what the mouth around them is turning into.

sentences.t:
Vox quoque iam rauca est, inflataque colla tumescunt,
ipsaque dilatant patulos convicia rictus.
sentences.l: The voice too is now hoarse, and the puffed-out necks swell, and the abuse itself widens their gaping jaws.
sentences.i: Their voices are hoarse now, their throats puff up and swell, and the insults themselves stretch their gaping mouths wider.
sentences.n: 'ipsa convicia' is the subject of 'dilatant': the abuse does the widening. This is the hinge of the whole metamorphosis — the vice is not merely punished by the change, it causes the change, pulling the mouth into a frog's. 'rictus' is the open jaw of an animal, a deliberately non-human word for a mouth.

sentences.t:
Terga caput tangunt, colla intercepta videntur,
spina viret, venter, pars maxima corporis, albet,
limosoque novae saliunt in gurgite ranae.””
sentences.l: The backs touch the head, the necks seem cut away, the spine is green, the belly, the largest part of the body, is white, and in the muddy pool new frogs leap.''
sentences.n: The naming is saved for the last word of the inset tale: 'ranae', frogs. Everything up to here has been anatomy — back, neck, spine, belly, colour — reported as though of a man being altered, and the noun arrives only when the change is finished. 'intercepta' is 'intercepted, taken away in between': the neck has not shrunk, it has been removed. 'novae' does double duty, 'new' and 'newly made'. 'Terga' is plural against a singular 'caput' — one head to each back. The edition prints two closing quotation marks here, because the host's speech and the bystander's frame end together, and the English closes both: the outer of the two shuts the tale that began at 317.
